themes.label: AI literacy and teaching AI use
Faculty and staff use of AI
Data, privacy, security and approved tools

types.name: Default stance: AI not allowed
types.name_v2: Prohibit AI on graded work by default
types.covers: The default rule bans generative AI on graded work (or on all work) in the course or unit.

types.name: Default stance: AI allowed or encouraged
types.name_v2: Permit or encourage AI by default
types.covers: The default rule allows, welcomes, encourages, or expects generative AI use.

types.name: Default stance: AI discouraged but not banned
types.name_v2: Discourage AI without forbidding it
types.covers: AI is discouraged or not recommended, but not formally prohibited.

types.name: Instructor or assignment decides AI use
types.name_v2: Let each instructor or assignment set the rule
types.covers: Whether AI is allowed is decided per instructor, per assignment, or per activity rather than by one rule.

types.name: Named levels or tiers of AI use
types.name_v2: Name explicit tiers or levels of AI use
types.covers: The policy defines named tiers, levels, colors, or categories of permitted AI use (e.g. no AI / limited / open), or a table of uses per assessment.

types.name: Fallback rule when no AI rule is stated
types.name_v2: Define the fallback rule when a syllabus is silent
types.covers: States what applies when a syllabus or assignment says nothing about AI (e.g. 'unless explicitly allowed, AI is prohibited').

types.name: AI built into everyday tools (writing assistants, editors, IDEs, agents)
types.name_v2: Cover AI built into editors, IDEs, and agents
types.covers: Rules that cover AI built into editors and IDEs (Copilot, Cursor, autocomplete), operating systems, browsers, or autonomous coding agents, including requiring students to disable them.

types.name: AI permission staged as skills or work develop
types.name_v2: Stage AI permission as skills develop
types.covers: AI permission changes over the course: forbidden early, allowed later once fundamentals are mastered or in later projects or advanced courses.

types.name: AI rules stated in the syllabus and assignment instructions
types.name_v2: Require an AI statement in every syllabus
types.covers: Instructors or departments must state AI expectations in the syllabus or assignment instructions.

types.name: Asking when unsure about AI use
types.name_v2: When unsure, students should ask before using AI
types.covers: Students who are unsure whether a use is allowed should ask the instructor first, or err on the side of not using AI.

types.name: AI rules vary by course; permission does not carry over
types.name_v2: Each course's policy governs only that course
types.covers: One course's AI permissions do not carry over to other courses or assignments.

types.name: AI as a tutor for concepts and background
types.name_v2: Allow AI as a tutor for understanding concepts
types.covers: AI may be used like a tutor or search engine to understand concepts, lecture material, or general questions, not to produce graded answers.

types.name: AI for debugging and explaining errors
types.name_v2: Allow AI to explain errors and help debug
types.covers: AI may be used to explain error messages, help debug, or clarify syntax.

types.name: AI for study and practice (quizzes, flashcards, review)
types.name_v2: Allow AI for practice, study aids, and review
types.covers: AI may be used to generate practice problems, study guides, summaries, reviews, or self-checks of knowledge.

types.name: AI for brainstorming and early planning
types.name_v2: Allow AI for brainstorming and exploring approaches
types.covers: AI may be used for brainstorming, idea generation, or exploring alternative approaches.

types.name: AI-generated content or code in submitted work
types.name_v2: Allow AI-generated code under stated conditions
types.covers: Students may submit or use AI-generated code under explicit conditions (small snippets, line or percentage caps, cited, specific projects, or freely).

types.name: Course-specific or institution-provided AI tools
types.name_v2: Provide a sanctioned, course-specific AI tool
types.covers: The course or university provides its own sanctioned AI tool (a course chatbot, tutor bot, or licensed assistant), sometimes the only AI allowed.

types.name: AI for writing versus AI for code (retired: split)
types.name_v2: Treat AI for prose separately from AI for code
types.covers: Specific rules for AI in prose and writing (reports, essays, comments, grammar or translation tools), separate from code.

types.name: Submitting AI-generated work as one's own
types.name_v2: Do not have AI produce the work you submit
types.covers: Students may not submit work that AI produced as their own (the student submits AI output). P140 covers the outsourcing frame, where AI is one of the outside parties that may not do the work.

types.name: Entering assignment questions or one's own work into AI
types.name_v2: Do not feed assignment specs or your code to AI
types.covers: Students may not paste or upload assignment specifications, questions, their own code, or the codebase into an AI tool.

types.name: AI for checking or debugging graded work
types.name_v2: Do not use AI to debug or check graded work
types.covers: Students may not use AI to debug, fix, proofread, reformat, or check graded work.

types.name: AI during exams, quizzes and in-class assessments
types.name_v2: No AI on exams, quizzes, or in-class assessments
types.covers: No AI on exams, quizzes, tests, or in-class assessments; closed-device rules during exams.

types.name: Keeping AI sessions separate from the submitted work
types.name_v2: Keep AI conversations apart from the work itself
types.covers: Keep AI conversations separate from the work: close the AI before writing, never copy-paste from it, never have both open, or use only browser chat interfaces.

types.name: Disclosing and acknowledging AI use
types.name_v2: Disclose AI use with each submission
types.covers: Students must disclose, acknowledge, or cite any AI use in their submission (a statement or citation).

types.name: What an AI citation or disclosure records (tool, prompt, output, format)
types.name_v2: Cite the tool, the prompt, and the output
types.covers: Citations of AI must include specific details such as the tool or model, the exact prompt, the output, or the date.

types.name: Process records: AI logs, drafts and reflections
types.name_v2: Keep and submit transcripts, logs, or reflections
types.covers: Students must keep and submit full transcripts, chat logs, journals, drafts, or reflections on their AI use.

types.name: Marking which parts of a submission are AI-derived
types.name_v2: Mark AI-derived code where it is used
types.covers: AI-derived code must be marked at the exact place it is used (code comments, README, acknowledgments file, top of file).

types.name: Nondisclosure as the violation
types.name_v2: Make disclosure safe and nondisclosure the violation
types.covers: How disclosure affects grading or integrity: disclosed use is not penalized, or failure to disclose is itself the violation (or, conversely, disclosed use is still penalized).

types.name: Submitted work must be one's own
types.name_v2: Students own everything they submit
types.covers: Students are responsible for and must own all work they submit; submitted work must be their own.

types.name: Explaining and defending one's own work
types.name_v2: Students must be able to explain every line
types.covers: Students must understand and be able to explain or defend every line and part of what they submit.

types.name: Verifying AI output
types.name_v2: Verify AI output; it is often wrong
types.covers: AI output can be wrong, biased, or hallucinated; students must verify and critically evaluate it.

types.name: AI supports, and does not replace, human thinking
types.name_v2: Students stay the primary problem-solver
types.covers: Students should remain the primary thinker and decision-maker; AI must not replace their thinking.

types.name: Supervised, proctored or in-class assessment
types.name_v2: Shift weight to proctored, unassisted assessment
types.covers: Assessment weight shifts toward proctored, in-class, or unassisted evaluation because of AI.

types.name: Explaining work orally (interviews, code reviews, presentations)
types.name_v2: Check understanding through code reviews, interviews, or oral exams
types.covers: Understanding is checked through code reviews, interviews, oral exams, demos, or meetings where students explain their work.

types.name: Assignment and assessment redesign for AI
types.name_v2: Redesign assignments and grading around AI
types.covers: Assignments, grading schemes, or course structure are redesigned around AI (e.g. two-pass submissions, grading on process or hours, baselines for declared AI use). Includes assignment-specific AI interaction protocols, e.g. a required prompt header (UIUC CS 128).

types.name: AI misuse as academic misconduct
types.name_v2: Treat unauthorized AI use as academic misconduct
types.covers: Unauthorized or improper AI use is classified as academic misconduct, plagiarism, or cheating and handled by integrity processes.

types.name: Consequences and sanctions for AI-rule violations
types.name_v2: State concrete penalties in advance
types.covers: Specific penalties for AI misuse are stated (zero, negative score, letter-grade reduction, course failure, escalation by offense).

types.name: Self-report, amnesty or leniency for inadvertent misuse
types.name_v2: Offer a self-report window or amnesty
types.covers: Students can self-report, withdraw a submission, or come forward within a window for reduced consequences.

types.name: Reliability and use of AI detectors
types.name_v2: Do not rely on AI detectors
types.covers: AI detectors are unreliable or will not be used or relied upon as proof.

types.name: Detection and similarity tools for AI misuse
types.name_v2: Use similarity checks and process evidence instead
types.covers: Similarity checking, plagiarism software, AI-detection tools, commit histories, or activity logs are used to identify misuse.

types.name: AI shortcuts the practice that builds skill
types.name_v2: Explain that AI shortcuts the practice that builds skill
types.covers: AI use is limited because doing the work yourself builds skill; outsourcing practice undermines learning.

types.name: Fundamentals before AI; protecting novices
types.name_v2: Protect novices; fundamentals come first
types.covers: Beginners and foundational courses especially need to learn fundamentals without AI; novices cannot judge AI output.

types.name: False sense of mastery from AI
types.name_v2: Warn that AI gives a false sense of mastery
types.covers: Relying on AI creates a false sense of mastery that is exposed on exams or later work.

types.name: Teaching AI use in courses
types.name_v2: Teach effective AI use as a professional skill
types.covers: Learning to use AI effectively is a professional skill employers expect; courses teach or demonstrate AI use.

types.name: AI under the existing rules for human help and sources
types.name_v2: Treat AI like a human collaborator under existing rules
types.covers: AI is treated like a human collaborator, peer, or outside source under existing collaboration or citation rules. Distinct from P140: P45 applies existing rules for human help or sources to AI; P140 names AI among the parties that may not do a student's work.

types.name: Human responsibility for grades
types.name_v2: Humans, not AI, assign grades
types.covers: Grades must be assigned by human instructors; AI will not grade or determine grades.

types.name: Instructor disclosure of their own AI and detector use
types.name_v2: Disclose instructor AI use to students
types.covers: Instructors disclose or describe their own use of AI (in grading, feedback, demos, or communication) to students, or commit to limits on it.

types.name: Disclosure and review of AI-made materials and communications
types.name_v2: Review and disclose AI-made course materials
types.covers: Course materials created with AI are disclosed and reviewed by instructors.

types.name: Uploading course materials and protected content to AI
types.name_v2: Do not upload course materials to AI tools
types.covers: Students may not upload course materials, assignment descriptions, or protected works into AI tools.

types.name: Keeping personal and sensitive data out of AI tools
types.name_v2: Protect personal data and prefer vetted tools
types.covers: Protect personal and confidential data; AI tools store prompts; prefer university-vetted or licensed tools.

types.name: Equitable access to AI (cost, alternatives, opt-out)
types.name_v2: Do not require paid tools; keep access equitable
types.covers: Equity and access: AI is optional or not required, free access is provided, paid tools are not required, accommodations and alternatives exist.

types.name: Copyright, intellectual property and terms of use
types.name_v2: Consider licensing and copyright of AI output
types.covers: Copyright, licensing, terms of use, and ownership of AI inputs and outputs.

types.name: Bias, fairness and general ethical concerns about AI
types.name_v2: Name bias, harms, and environmental costs
types.covers: Ethical, bias, labor, and environmental concerns about AI.

types.name: Policy review and revision over time
types.name_v2: Revisit the policy regularly
types.covers: The policy is provisional and will be revisited, revised, or updated; feedback is invited.

types.name: Evidence on AI use and its effects
types.name_v2: Gather evidence on how AI affects learning
types.covers: Evidence or data about how AI use affects student learning or performance is collected or cited.

types.name: Institutional values and principles for AI use
types.name_v2: Set an institution-wide framework for responsible AI use
types.covers: An institution-level framework or preamble stating the purpose, scope, and principles for AI use.

types.name: Instructor-student conversation before escalating suspected misuse
types.name_v2: Talk with the student before escalating suspected misuse
types.covers: Instructors should talk with the student and gather context before escalating suspected AI misuse.

types.name: Students' own course communication (posts, messages)
types.name_v2: Students write their own course communication
types.covers: Messages, emails or posts that students send to course staff must be written by the student, not generated by AI (source: UC Irvine ICS 33/H32).

types.name: Instructor AI use for teaching work
types.name_v2: Instructor use of AI for teaching work
types.covers: What instructors or staff may, should or should not use AI for in their own teaching work: drafting syllabi, rubrics, quiz items, examples, feedback drafts, translations, letters. Final grading decisions are P46; disclosure to students is P47; AI-made course materials are P48 (sources: UIUC CITL and Grainger; Oregon State EECS).

types.name: Trust and course design over policing AI use
types.name_v2: Decline to police AI use
types.covers: Staff state they will not actively police or detect AI use, relying instead on unassisted assessments or student responsibility (source: UIUC ECE 220).

types.name: Definitions and scope of the policy
types.name_v2: Define AI and the policy's scope
types.covers: Definitions of AI, generative AI, AI tools or agentic systems that set what a policy covers (sources: Oregon State, Howard).

types.name: AI in research, publication and review
types.name_v2: Govern AI use in research and scholarship
types.covers: AI rules for theses, dissertations, manuscripts, grants and peer review, including deferring to venue, funder, sponsor or IRB rules (sources: Oregon State EECS, Howard Policy 100-022).

types.name: Faculty support and learning about AI
types.name_v2: Support faculty in learning AI
types.covers: Workshops, consultations, faculty communities, and advice that instructors try AI tools and learn their implications before setting course policy (sources: Oregon State, Howard).

types.name: Due process for students accused of misuse
types.name_v2: Students may respond to AI-misuse allegations
types.covers: Students accused of AI misuse have a right to respond or present evidence; fairness and transparency in AI-related integrity cases (source: Howard).

types.name: Review and approval of AI tools and vendors
types.name_v2: Review and approve AI tools, vendors and data sharing
types.covers: Institutional review of AI contracts and partnerships, and limits on licensing or sharing university data and IP with AI providers (source: Howard Policy 100-022). Broadened 2026-10-26 (D33): also covers review and approval of any AI tool or system before purchase or deployment (security, risk, accessibility, legal), and periodic re-evaluation of approved tools. Evidence: Morehouse, Old Dominion, Rutgers (3), Santa Clara, Oakland, Penn State, Northwestern, Purdue.

types.name: Explaining and discussing AI rules with students
types.name_v2: Explain and discuss the AI rules with students
types.covers: Instructors give students the reasons behind their AI rules, discuss AI in class, or word the rules with care (tone, avoiding anthropomorphic language), going beyond listing the rule in the syllabus. Evidence before adding: Carleton, Brown, Boston College, Case Western, IU Indianapolis, Binghamton, George Mason, Michigan State.

types.name: Co-creating course AI policy with students
types.name_v2: Co-create the AI policy with students
types.covers: Instructors set the course's AI expectations together with students, for example through class discussion, to build understanding and buy-in. Evidence: Cal Poly Pomona, Cal State LA, Georgetown, Georgia State.

types.name: Educative response to misuse
types.name_v2: Respond to misuse educatively, not only punitively
types.covers: Treat suspected or confirmed AI misuse, especially first offenses, as a learning opportunity; prefer educative or remedial responses; presume good faith; reduce the pressures that lead to cheating. Different from P60 (declining to police) and P57 (talking before escalating). Evidence: Austin CC, East Tennessee State, Florida State, IU Indianapolis, George Washington, Clemson, Case Western.

types.name: Evidence standards for AI-misuse findings
types.name_v2: Set evidence standards for AI-misuse findings
types.covers: What evidence is needed, or not sufficient, to find AI misuse: a standard of proof, the kinds of evidence to weigh, or the statement that a hunch that work 'does not sound like the student' is not enough. Evidence: Cornell, Grinnell, Iowa State, Clark, Georgetown. Broadened 2026-10-26 (D33): also covers rules that detector output may be used only as supporting evidence, not as proof. Evidence: Oberlin, Rice, Santa Clara, Old Dominion, Rowan.

types.name: AI literacy training and resources
types.name_v2: Provide or require AI training for students and staff
types.covers: The institution offers or mandates AI-literacy training, modules, guides or curricular AI-literacy for students, staff or the whole community. Faculty-only support is P63. Evidence: Georgia Southern, Kennesaw State, Clark, East Tennessee State, Florida International, Brown, Baylor, Cleveland State.

types.name: Reporting AI incidents and misuse
types.name_v2: Report AI incidents, data exposure and misuse
types.covers: A duty or channel to report AI-related problems: accidental exposure of sensitive data, tool malfunctions, policy violations or misconduct by others. Evidence: Augusta, Case Western, Georgia State, Kansas State, Marquette.

types.name: Contact points and human help for AI questions
types.name_v2: Point students to human help alongside AI
types.covers: Students are directed to instructors, librarians, writing centers, advisors or other human support, alongside or instead of AI tools. Evidence: Marquette, Harvey Mudd, Cal State, Florida International, BYU, Clemson.

types.name: Human oversight of AI-influenced decisions
types.name_v2: Keep humans responsible for decisions about people
types.covers: AI may not be the sole basis for consequential decisions about individuals, such as hiring, admissions, discipline, evaluation or academic standing; a human reviews and decides. Grading alone is P46. Evidence: Austin CC, Clark, Colby, Hampton, Michigan State.

types.name: Harmful, deceptive or fabricating AI uses
types.name_v2: Ban deceptive, fabricated or malicious AI use
types.covers: General conduct rules against using AI to deceive, impersonate, fabricate or falsify data or records, harass, spread misinformation, write malware or breach security. Evidence: Cal State, East Tennessee State, George Mason, Kansas State, LSU, Michigan State, Colby.

types.name: AI-enabled phishing and security threats
types.name_v2: Guard against AI-enabled phishing and security threats
types.covers: Security awareness: watch for AI-crafted phishing, scams and deepfakes, and report suspicious messages. Evidence: Bowdoin, Bucknell, Colby, East Carolina, Georgia Tech, Howard, Lamar.

types.name: Administrative and operational AI use
types.name_v2: Govern administrative and operational AI use
types.covers: Rules for AI in university operations outside teaching, such as staff administrative work, student services, official communications, chatbots or AI-built apps shared with others. Evidence: Brandeis, Hampton, Davidson, Kansas State, DePaul, Cal State.

types.name: Existing law and university policy apply to AI
types.name_v2: Comply with existing law and university policy
types.covers: AI use must follow laws (records, privacy, IP) and existing university policies (conduct, acceptable use, branding), and violations fall under those policies. Different from P45, which treats AI like a human collaborator under integrity rules. Evidence: Amherst, Boise State, Kansas State, Arizona State, Cal State, Davidson.

types.name: Finding out and following each course's AI rules
types.name_v2: Students learn and follow each course's AI rules
types.covers: Students are responsible for finding out, reading and following the AI rules that apply to them in each course, program or assignment (check the syllabus first). Different from P10 (ask when unsure) and P11 (a course's rule binds only that course). Evidence: Georgetown, Harvey Mudd, Rutgers-Camden, Rutgers-Newark, Princeton, Oakland, San José State, NIU, Northwestern, NAU, Portland State.

types.name: AI use built into coursework
types.name_v2: Require AI use in some coursework
types.covers: AI use is built into, expected in or required for an assignment or course, or instructors are told they may require it. Evidence: Ohio State, RIT, Brown, Oregon State, Pepperdine, Oakland, Northeastern, Sam Houston State.

types.name: Governance roles, ownership and exceptions
types.name_v2: Name who owns, enforces and grants exceptions to the AI policy
types.covers: Names the office, officer, council or committee that interprets, implements, monitors or enforces the AI policy, or the process for granting exceptions to it. Evidence: Purdue, Rowan, Oakland, Morehouse, Northeastern, Northwestern, Portland State, Santa Clara.

types.name: Formal integrity procedure (reporting, referral, sanctions process)
types.name_v2: Follow the formal integrity-reporting procedure
types.covers: Procedural steps once misuse is suspected or sanctioned: instructors file a report with a central office, meet deadlines, use a required form, and leave sanctions to the deciding body. Different from P36 (classifying misuse as misconduct) and P57 (talking with the student first). Evidence: San José State, RPI, Rowan, SMU, Santa Clara, Oregon State, Rice, Oberlin, Portland State.

types.name: Limits of preventing and detecting AI use
types.name_v2: Acknowledge that AI use cannot be fully prevented or verified
types.covers: States limits on control: bans are impractical or counterproductive, AI use cannot be fully eliminated, faculty cannot always verify originality, assessments lose reliability. Evidence: Rush, NC A&T, Oregon State, RIT, MIT, NC State.

types.name: AI decisions grounded in learning objectives
types.name_v2: Align AI decisions with learning objectives
types.covers: Whether and how AI is allowed should follow from the course's or program's learning objectives. Evidence: Rush, Northeastern, Case Western, SF State, Morehouse, Santa Clara, Middle Tennessee State.

types.name: How the policy was made (body, process, sources, AI assistance)
types.name_v2: Describe how and by whom the policy was made
types.covers: States the process, body or date by which the AI policy or guidance was drafted, consulted on, adopted or ratified. Evidence: New Mexico State, Rice, Northeastern, Santa Clara.

types.name: Units set their own AI rules
types.name_v2: Let schools or units set their own AI rules
types.covers: Colleges, schools, departments or programs may set their own or additional AI rules, or have different expectations from the university-wide rule. P04 is the instructor-level version. Evidence: Santa Clara, Saint Louis, Northeastern, San Diego State, Purdue, Middle Tennessee State, SMU.

types.name: Consent for AI recording, transcription and likeness
types.name_v2: Require consent before AI recording or transcription
types.covers: Class sessions or meetings may not be recorded or transcribed by AI tools without permission or announcement. Evidence: Augusta, Kean, Oregon State, Santa Clara.

types.name: Benefits of AI for learning and teaching
types.name_v2: State the benefits of AI for learning
types.covers: Names benefits of AI for teaching and learning (personalization, accessibility, efficiency, creativity) without making it a rule or a career-skill claim (P44). Evidence: New Mexico State, LSU, Ohio State, NC State, Prairie View A&M, Rush, SF State.

types.name: Engaging peers, partners and the community on AI
types.name_v2: Engage peers, partners and the community on AI
types.covers: Coalitions with other universities, benchmarking against peers, partnerships with industry or government, and public forums on AI. Evidence: Brown, EVMS, Kansas State, Old Dominion.

types.name: AI for data analysis and visualization
types.name_v2: Allow AI for data analysis and visualization
types.covers: AI may be used to analyze, sort, simulate or visualize data. Evidence: Ohio State, Morehouse, FIU, SMU, NAU, Sam Houston State.

types.name: Own attempt first, then AI
types.name_v2: Do the work yourself first, then use AI
types.covers: A sequencing rule: the student first attempts, drafts or develops the work without AI, and AI help is allowed only afterward. Evidence: Ohio State, North Dakota State, Oregon State, Northwestern.

types.name: AI for editing, proofreading and outlining one's own work
types.name_v2: Allow AI for editing, proofreading and writing support
types.covers: AI may help with editing, proofreading, grammar, outlining, organizing or revising one's own writing. P18 is about treating prose differently from code; this is the permission itself. Evidence: Morehouse, Rutgers, NAU, Ohio State, Oakland, Rowan, Penn State, Rush, NC State.

types.name: University-licensed or approved AI tools
types.name_v2: Use university-licensed or approved AI tools
types.covers: Use the AI tools the university licenses, provides or approves (institution-wide, not one course: that is P17), or know the approved list. Evidence: NYU, Morehouse, Rutgers (3 campuses), SUNY ESF, RIT, Nova Southeastern, Rowan, NC State.

types.name: Prompting advice
types.name_v2: Advise on how to prompt AI effectively
types.covers: Practical advice on writing prompts or probing AI tools to get better results or learn their limits. Evidence: Pepperdine, Oakland, Sam Houston State, Santa Clara, San Diego State, NC State.

types.name: Careers and professional norms as reasons to build skills without AI
types.name_v2: Cite careers as a reason to build skills without AI
types.covers: The reason given for limiting AI is professional readiness: employers expect skills, critical thinking or work in settings without AI. P44 is the opposite argument (learn AI for careers). Evidence: Oregon State, RIT, Santa Clara, Princeton.

types.name: Integrity, honesty and fairness as grounds for AI rules
types.name_v2: Ground AI limits in fairness and academic honesty
types.covers: The reason given for AI rules is fairness to other students, honest evaluation, or the integrity culture of the community, not skill-building (P41). Evidence: CUNY Graduate Center, Santa Clara, Prairie View A&M, Northeastern Illinois, San José State, Oberlin.

types.name: AI is not an author, source or collaborator
types.name_v2: Treat AI as neither author, source nor collaborator
types.covers: AI is not a person: it cannot be an author, a cited source or a group member, and AI use is not acceptable collaboration. The opposite of P45. Evidence: Princeton, Pepperdine, Santa Clara.

types.name: Accessibility and AI
types.name_v2: Make AI use and output accessible
types.covers: Accessibility of AI tools and AI-produced materials for people with disabilities: accessibility reviews, alternative access plans, accessible output, AI as an accessibility aid. P51 covers cost and equal access. Evidence: Nova Southeastern, Ohio State, Penn State, Oregon State, Santa Clara, NAU.

types.name: Documenting, auditing and monitoring AI systems
types.name_v2: Document, audit and monitor deployed AI systems
types.covers: Institutional AI systems are documented (model cards, records), audited or monitored for bias, accuracy, security and drift over time. Evidence: Morehouse, Georgia Southern, Old Dominion, Saint Louis, Oakland, Northwestern.

types.name: Reducing pressures that lead to misuse
types.name_v2: Reduce the pressures that lead to AI misuse
types.covers: Prevention by easing the causes of misuse: extensions, office hours, support resources, time management, explaining assignment purposes. P68 is the response after misuse. Evidence: Clemson, Rice, Old Dominion, IU Indianapolis, BYU.

types.name: Routine or minor AI uses outside the rules
types.name_v2: Exempt routine AI features from the rules
types.covers: Routine embedded features (spell-check, grammar check, search, autocomplete) are allowed or need no disclosure even under a restrictive rule. Evidence: Oregon State, Morehouse, Pepperdine.

types.name: AI in grading and feedback by instructors
types.name_v2: Set conditions for AI-assisted grading
types.covers: AI-assisted grading or feedback is allowed only under conditions: approval chains, explainability, human review of AI-drafted feedback, closed-form only. P46 is the rule that only humans assign grades. Evidence: Penn State, Purdue, Northeastern, SMU, Old Dominion, Oregon State.

types.name: Staying informed about AI developments
types.name_v2: Stay informed about AI developments and guidance
types.covers: A duty or encouragement for users to keep up with AI developments, best practices and the institution's current AI guidance. Evidence: East Tennessee State, San Diego State, NAU.

types.name: Notice when AI is used in interactions or decisions
types.name_v2: Tell people when they are interacting with AI
types.covers: People have a right to know when they are dealing with an AI system (chatbots, deployed systems), including its scope and limits. P47 is instructor disclosure to students. Evidence: Northwestern, Cal State, Morehouse.

types.name: AI for literature search and finding sources
types.name_v2: Allow AI for literature search and finding sources
types.covers: AI may help find, screen or annotate sources and literature, usually on condition that the student reads and verifies them. Evidence: idaho, rowan, tennessee-state, new-school, tulane.

types.name: AI for reading and summarizing sources
types.name_v2: Ban AI for reading and summarizing sources
types.covers: Students may not use AI to summarize, contextualize or digest assigned readings or source material, even when no AI output is submitted (a ban on study use, the opposite of P14). Evidence: arizona, nevada-reno, texas-christian, brandeis.

types.name: AI for images and multimedia
types.name_v2: Allow AI for images and illustrations
types.covers: AI may generate figures, illustrations, storyboards or graphics, often only if they contain no data. Evidence: rowan, stony-brook, alabama-huntsville, nebraska-lincoln, louisiana-lafayette.

types.name: Prior approval or a closed list of permitted uses
types.name_v2: Require prior approval or limit AI to listed tasks
types.covers: AI is allowed only after explicit prior approval (sometimes a written proposal of the intended use) or only for a closed list of tasks. P10 is asking when unsure; P05 names tiers. Evidence: seton-hall, teachers-college-columbia, vermont, unc-charlotte, texas-health-science-center-houston.

types.name: No institution-wide AI policy exists
types.name_v2: State that no specific AI policy exists
types.covers: The document says the institution (or its integrity policy) has no AI-specific or uniform policy, often as the reason decisions fall to instructors. Evidence: william-and-mary, nevada-las-vegas, central-florida, seton-hall, maryland-baltimore-county.

types.name: Aligning AI rules across sections, departments and disciplines
types.name_v2: Coordinate AI rules across sections, departments and disciplines
types.covers: Instructors should align AI rules and penalties with colleagues, across sections of one course, or with their discipline's norms, so students meet consistent rules. P85 is units setting their own rules. Evidence: temple, kansas, louisville, delaware, california-riverside, colorado-state, northeastern.

types.name: Sample syllabus language and templates
types.name_v2: Provide sample syllabus language and templates
types.covers: The institution supplies sample AI syllabus statements or templates for instructors to adopt. P63 is helping faculty learn about AI. Evidence: maryland-baltimore-county, tennessee-technological, maryland-baltimore.

types.name: Integrity pledges and signed AI agreements
types.name_v2: Have students sign an integrity pledge or AI agreement
types.covers: Students sign or reaffirm an honor code, integrity pledge or AI-use agreement, per course, per assessment or per term. Evidence: seton-hall, delaware, california-santa-cruz, california-san-diego, syracuse, florida-international.

types.name: Instructors modeling responsible AI use
types.name_v2: Instructors model responsible AI use
types.covers: Instructors' own AI use and mentorship are framed as teaching responsible use by example. P59 is instructor AI use for teaching work. Evidence: william-and-mary, texas-tech, texas-aandm.

types.name: Institutional monitoring of AI use
types.name_v2: Reserve the right to monitor AI use
types.covers: The institution may access, review or audit prompts, outputs and accounts on its AI tools; users have no expectation of privacy there. Evidence: maryland-college-park, maryland-baltimore, nevada-reno.

types.name: Personal responsibility for self-chosen AI tools
types.name_v2: Users bear responsibility for AI tools they sign up for
types.covers: People who accept an AI tool's terms or use unlicensed tools on their own carry the risk and liability; the institution disclaims guarantees. Evidence: maryland-college-park, maryland-baltimore, texas-medical-branch-galveston, nevada-reno, louisville.

types.name: Pointers to further AI guidance and resources
types.name_v2: Point to further AI guidance and resources
types.covers: The document directs readers to other pages, guides or offices for AI rules, citation formats or support. P72 is human help for students. Evidence: tennessee-technological, ohio-state, arkansas, dayton.

types.name: General expectation of ethical, responsible use
types.name_v2: State a general expectation of ethical, responsible use
types.covers: A general call to use AI ethically and responsibly with no specific content; kept so such statements are counted but not overread. Evidence: texas-dallas, massachusetts-boston, south-florida, minnesota, southern.

types.name: Evaluating an AI tool before choosing it
types.name_v2: Evaluate an AI tool and choose one suited to the task
types.covers: Users should research, test or assess a tool (accuracy, trustworthiness, fit to the task) before choosing it. P65 is institutional review and approval. Evidence: swarthmore-college, colorado-colorado-springs, seattle, colorado-boulder, northeastern.

types.name: Weighing benefits and risks before using AI
types.name_v2: Weigh benefits, risks and values before using AI
types.covers: Users decide whether to use AI by weighing its gains, risks, ethics and their own values in context. Evidence: maryland-baltimore, seton-hall, alaska-fairbanks, colorado-boulder, unc-charlotte, tulane, nevada-las-vegas.

types.name: AI for career and personal tasks outside coursework
types.name_v2: Allow AI for career and personal tasks outside coursework
types.covers: AI suggested or allowed for job preparation, career planning or everyday personal tasks, sometimes with a note to check employers' rules. Evidence: tennessee-state, syracuse, central-florida, swarthmore-college.

types.name: Fabricated citations and unattributed sources in AI output
types.name_v2: Warn that AI output can cause unintentional plagiarism
types.covers: AI reproduces sources without attribution, so using its output risks unintentional plagiarism or fabrication. Evidence: new-school, colorado-boulder, massachusetts-lowell.

types.name: AI displacing human interaction and feedback
types.name_v2: Warn that AI can displace human interaction and feedback
types.covers: Overreliance on AI can reduce contact with instructors and peers or replace human feedback that learning depends on. Evidence: cornell, alabama-birmingham, texas-austin.

types.name: Institutional investment in AI capacity
types.name_v2: Invest in AI research, infrastructure and capacity
types.covers: Institutional commitments to AI research centers, computing resources, funding or collaboration; not rules on AI use. Evidence: tennessee-technological, louisville, william-and-mary, tulane, arkansas-little-rock.

types.name: Telling students how misuse will be detected and handled
types.name_v2: Say how misuse will be detected and handled
types.covers: Course policies should state how AI misuse will be detected and how it will be handled. P36 classes misuse as misconduct; P37 states penalties. Evidence: kansas, nevada-las-vegas, uc-irvine, purdue, santa-clara.

types.name: Consistent and transparent application of AI rules
types.name_v2: Apply AI rules consistently and transparently
types.covers: Instructors apply their AI expectations the same way to all students and make them transparent. Evidence: uc-irvine, middle-tennessee-state, boston.

types.name: Students checking their own work for similarity or AI
types.name_v2: Let students check their own work for similarity or AI
types.covers: Students are offered or pointed to tools to check their own drafts for similarity or AI-generated text before submitting. Evidence: arkansas-little-rock, boston, oregon-state.

types.name: Security of AI accounts, systems and AI-written code
types.name_v2: Secure AI accounts and systems
types.covers: Security controls for AI accounts and systems: multi-factor authentication, credentials, patching, access limits and controls on AI agents. P75 is AI-enabled threats. Evidence: texas-san-antonio, ut-rio-grande-valley, houston, morehouse-college.

types.name: AI in group work
types.name_v2: Set AI rules for group work
types.covers: Rules for AI use in group projects: members agree on use, say what to do if one member uses AI, or share responsibility for a violation. Evidence: washington, arizona-state, north-carolina-state.

types.name: AI for translation and language support
types.covers: Rules on using AI to translate text or to support language learning (permitted, conditioned or banned). Split out of P18 and from reviewer NEW labels.

types.name: AI feedback or critique on one's own work
types.covers: Using AI to get feedback, critique or review of one's own draft, code or solution (not to produce it). From P14, P91 subgroups and NEW labels.

types.name: Signs and indicators of AI-written work
types.covers: Manual signs, comparisons and indicators instructors use to suspect AI-written work (style shifts, fabricated citations, comparison with earlier work), as distinct from detector tools (P40) and standards of proof (P69).

types.name: What AI can and cannot do (capabilities and limits)
types.covers: Statements about AI's capabilities and limits beyond wrong output (P31): low quality, shallow reasoning, changing capability, what tools are and are not good for.

types.name: Status of the guidance (advisory or binding, precedence)
types.covers: The document says whether it is guidance or binding policy, and which text prevails when guidance and formal policy conflict.

types.name: Accountability for AI-assisted output
types.covers: Users are responsible for the accuracy, quality and consequences of AI-assisted work they submit or use (split from P29, which keeps 'submitted work must be one's own').

types.name: Career and workplace readiness as a reason to learn AI
types.covers: Preparing students for an AI-shaped workplace as the rationale for teaching or allowing AI (split from P44, which keeps teaching AI use in courses).

types.name: Environmental cost of AI
types.covers: Energy, water and carbon costs of AI named as a concern (split from P53).

types.name: Labor, consent and credit behind AI
types.covers: Concerns about uncredited labor, training on work without consent, and exploitation in building AI (split from P53).

types.name: AI records retention and public-records duties
types.covers: AI prompts, outputs and logs as records subject to retention rules or public-records requests.

types.name: AI is widespread and here to stay
types.covers: Context statements that AI is inevitable, already widespread or here to stay, used to frame the policy.

types.name: Purpose and context of the policy document
types.covers: Why the document exists, what problem it addresses and its context (split from P56, which keeps values and principles).

types.name: Having another person or AI do your course work
types.covers: Outsourcing: students may not have another person, entity, service or AI do their work for a course (the outside party does the work, as in contract cheating). Split from P19 on PI review (D58).

alpha.note: Coder A and Coder B coded independently with the same codebook version; pairs matched by anchor-span overlap >= 50%.

examples: Generative AI means AI systems that create new content such as text, images, audio, video or code.
The policy applies to all members of the university community, including students, faculty, staff and affiliates.
Artificial intelligence means computer systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence.
The policy covers academic work such as coursework, teaching, research, theses and assessments.
The university encourages and supports responsible exploration, experimentation and use of AI by its community.
Everyone remains responsible for the content they produce with AI; responsibility cannot shift to the tool.
These policies provide a framework for the responsible and ethical use of AI.
Everyone uses AI to support, not replace, human judgment, critical thinking and creativity.
AI output can be inaccurate, biased or fabricated, and students should be aware of this.
AI rules differ across courses and instructors, so students check each course's expectations.
AI tools may store, reuse or train on what users enter, so entered information may not stay private.
Using AI can replace, bypass or shortcut the practice and work through which students learn and build skills.
The university provides licensed AI tools to its students, faculty and staff.
University-approved AI tools are vetted and protect entered data, including from model training.
A named committee, task force or working group, convened or charged by university leaders, drafted the AI policy or guidance.
The university provides no AI detection tool.
Generative AI means any text, image or code generating system; course-built models and all coursework are covered or exempted as stated.
Integrity policies cover students' agent session transcripts and the activity their hooks report.
Having AI do the work undermines learning, which comes from doing the work yourself.
Fundamentals must be mastered before relying on AI, and unaided programming remains a core learning goal.
The course is designed to build students' own skills, understanding and independent problem-solving.
AI is a valuable and helpful tool for learning the material.
AI output, code and explanations can be wrong, inaccurate, hallucinated, incomplete or misleading.
Relying on AI for homework leaves students unprepared and hurts their performance on exams.
AI use or reliance hinders students' own critical, creative and independent thinking.
Employers assess job candidates without AI, and interviews do not allow AI, so unaided skills matter.
